{{Short description|Type of discrete orthogonal polynomials}}
{{distinguish|Chebyshev polynomials}}
In mathematics, '''discrete Chebyshev polynomials''', or '''Gram polynomials''', are a type of [[discrete orthogonal polynomials]] used in [[approximation theory]], introduced by [[Pafnuty Chebyshev]]<ref name="chebyshev">{{citation |last=Chebyshev|first=P. |title=Sur l'interpolation |journal=Zapiski Akademii Nauk |volume=4|year=1864|id=Oeuvres Vol 1 p. 539–560 |url=https://archive.org/stream/oeuvresdepltche01chebrich#page/n551/mode/2up }}</ref> and rediscovered by [[Jørgen Pedersen Gram|Gram]].<ref name="gram">{{Citation | last1=Gram | first1=J. P. | title=Ueber die Entwickelung reeller Functionen in Reihen mittelst der Methode der kleinsten Quadrate | url=http://resolver.sub.uni-goettingen.de/purl?GDZPPN002158604 | language=German | jfm=15.0321.03 | year=1883 | journal=Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik | volume=1883 | issue=94 | pages=41–73 | doi=10.1515/crll.1883.94.41| s2cid=116847377 | url-access=subscription }}</ref> They were later found to be applicable to various algebraic properties of spin [[angular momentum]]. This connection shows that they can be expressed as Clebsch-Gordan coefficients.

==Elementary definition==

The discrete Chebyshev polynomial <math>t^N_n(x)</math> is a polynomial of degree ''n'' in ''x'', for <math> n = 0, 1, 2,\ldots, N -1</math>, constructed such that two polynomials of unequal degree are orthogonal with respect to the weight function
<math display="block"> w(x) = \sum_{r = 0}^{N-1} \delta(x-r),</math>
with <math>\delta(\cdot)</math> being the [[Dirac delta function]]. That is,
<math display="block"> \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} t^N_n(x) t^N_m (x) w(x) \, dx = 0 \quad \text{ if } \quad n \ne m .</math>

The integral on the left is actually a sum because of the delta function, and we have,
<math display="block"> \sum_{r = 0}^{N-1} t^N_n(r) t^N_m (r) = 0 \quad \text{ if }\quad n \ne m. </math>

Thus, even though <math>t^N_n(x)</math> is a polynomial in <math>x</math>, only its values at a discrete set of points,
<math> x = 0, 1, 2, \ldots, N-1 </math> are of any significance. Nevertheless, because these polynomials can be defined in terms of orthogonality with respect to a nonnegative [[weight function]], the entire theory of orthogonal polynomials is applicable. In particular, the polynomials are complete in the sense that
<math display="block"> \sum_{n = 0}^{N-1} t^N_n(r) t^N_n (s) = 0 \quad \text{ if }\quad r \ne s. </math>

Chebyshev chose the normalization so that
<math display="block"> \sum_{r = 0}^{N-1} t^N_n(r) t^N_n (r) = \frac{N}{2n+1} \prod_{k=1}^n (N^2 - k^2). </math>

This fixes the polynomials completely along with the [[sign convention]], <math> t^N_n(N - 1) > 0</math>.

If the independent variable is linearly scaled and shifted so that the end points assume the values <math>-1</math> and <math>1</math>, then as <math>N \to \infty </math>, <math>t^N_n(\cdot) \to P_n(\cdot)</math> times a constant, where <math>P_n</math> is the Legendre polynomial.

==Advanced definition==

Let {{math|''f''}} be a [[smooth function]] defined on the [[closed interval]] [&minus;1,&nbsp;1], whose values are known explicitly only at points {{math|1=''x''<sub>''k''</sub> := −1 + (2''k'' − 1)/''m''}}, where ''k'' and ''m'' are [[integers]] and {{math|1 &le; ''k'' &le; ''m''}}. The task is to approximate ''f'' as a [[polynomial]] of degree ''n'' < ''m''. Consider a [[Positive semidefinite function|positive semi-definite]] [[bilinear form]]
<math display="block">\left(g,h\right)_d:=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{k=1}^{m}{g(x_k)h(x_k)},</math>
where {{math|''g''}} and {{math|''h''}} are [[Continuous function|continuous]] on [&minus;1,&nbsp;1] and let
<math display="block">\left\|g\right\|_d:=(g,g)^{1/2}_{d} </math>
be a discrete [[semi-norm]]. Let <math>\varphi_k</math> be a [[Indexed family|family]] of polynomials orthogonal to each other
<math display="block">\left( \varphi_k, \varphi_i\right)_d = 0</math>
whenever {{mvar|i}} is not equal to {{mvar|k}}. Assume all the polynomials <math>\varphi_k</math> have a positive [[leading coefficient]] and they are [[Unit vector|normalized]] in such a way that
<math display="block">\left\|\varphi_k\right\|_d=1.</math>

The <math>\varphi_k</math> are called discrete Chebyshev (or Gram) polynomials.<ref>{{cite journal
| author = R.W. Barnard |author2=G. Dahlquist |author3=K. Pearce |author4=L. Reichel |author5=K.C. Richards
| title = Gram Polynomials and the Kummer Function
| journal = [[Journal of Approximation Theory]]
| year = 1998
| volume = 94
| pages = 128&ndash;143
| doi = 10.1006/jath.1998.3181
| doi-access = free
}}</ref>

==Connection with spin algebra==

The discrete Chebyshev polynomials have surprising connections to various algebraic properties of spin: spin transition probabilities,<ref>{{cite journal
| author = A. Meckler
| title = Majorana formula
| journal = Physical Review
| year = 1958
| volume = 111
| issue = 6
| page = 1447
| doi = 10.1103/PhysRev.111.1447
| bibcode = 1958PhRv..111.1447M
}}</ref>
the probabilities for observations of the spin in [[David Bohm|Bohm's]] spin-s version of the [[EPR paradox|Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen]] experiment,<ref>{{cite journal
| author = N. D. Mermin | author2 = G. M. Schwarz
| title = Joint distributions and local realism in the higher-spin Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen experiment
| journal = Foundations of Physics
| year = 1982
| volume = 12
| issue = 2
| page = 101
| doi = 10.1007/BF00736844
| bibcode = 1982FoPh...12..101M
| s2cid = 121648820
}}</ref>
and [[Wigner quasiprobability distribution|Wigner functions]] for various spin states.<ref>{{cite journal
| author = Anupam Garg
| title = The discrete Chebyshev–Meckler–Mermin–Schwarz polynomials and spin algebra
| journal = Journal of Mathematical Physics
| year = 2022
| volume = 63
| issue = 7
| page = 072101
| doi = 10.1063/5.0094575
| bibcode = 2022JMP....63g2101G
}}</ref>

Specifically, the polynomials turn out to be the eigenvectors of the absolute square of the [[rotation matrix]] (the [[Wigner D-matrix]]). The associated eigenvalue is the Legendre polynomial <math>P_{\ell}(\cos \theta)</math>, where <math>\theta</math> is the rotation angle. In other words, if
<math display="block"> d_{mm'} = \langle j,m|e^{-i\theta J_y}|j,m'\rangle,</math>
where <math> |j,m\rangle </math> are the usual angular momentum or spin eigenstates,
and
<math display="block"> F_{mm'}(\theta) = |d_{mm'}(\theta)|^2 ,</math>
then
<math display="block"> \sum_{m' = -j}^j F_{mm'}(\theta)\, f^j_{\ell}(m')= P_{\ell}(\cos\theta) f^j_{\ell}(m) .</math>

The eigenvectors <math> f^j_{\ell}(m)</math> are scaled and shifted versions of the Chebyshev polynomials. They are shifted so as to have support on the points <math> m = -j, -j + 1, \ldots, j</math> instead of <math> r = 0, 1, \ldots, N</math> for <math> t^N_n(r) </math> with <math>N</math> corresponding to <math> 2j+1 </math>, and <math>n</math> corresponding to <math>\ell</math>. In addition, the <math> f^j_{\ell}(m)</math> can be scaled so as to obey other normalization conditions. For example, one could demand that they satisfy
<math display="block"> \frac{1}{2j+1} \sum_{m=-j}^{j} f^j_{\ell}(m) f^j_{\ell'}(m) = \delta_{\ell\ell'},</math>
along with <math> f^j_{\ell}(j) > 0 </math>.


==Connection with Clebsch-Gordan coefficients==

In the form, <math> f^j_{\ell}(m)</math>, the connection with spin algebra shows that these polynomials are Clebsch-Gordan coefficients. To be consistent with the normalization given above, the relation is

<math display="block">
f^j_{\ell}(m) = (-1)^{j - m} \sqrt{2j+1} \langle{j\,j\,\ell\,0|j,m; j,-m}\rangle.
</math>
